summary: A vineyard owner hires workers throughout the day and pays each a full daily wage, provoking those hired first to resent generosity. Jesus again predicts betrayal, condemnation, mockery, flogging, death, and resurrection. The mother of James and John asks for royal seats, and Jesus turns the rank dispute into cup, service, and the Son of Man's ransom. Leaving Jericho, two blind men call him Son of David; the crowd tries to silence them, but compassion stops the journey and restores their sight.
whyItMatters: The chapter dismantles comparison-based entitlement and prestige. Kingdom generosity is not controlled by the longest résumé; greatness is service rather than proximity to power; and the royal Son of David hears the people a moving crowd treats as noise.

context.author: Anonymous narrator continuing the road to Jerusalem
context.audience: Disciples and communities tempted by seniority, reward, and hierarchical honor
context.setting: Vineyard parable, road upward to Jerusalem, and departure from Jericho
context.literaryForm: Kingdom parable, passion prediction, status controversy, and healing

keyVerses.text: So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.”
keyVerses.why: The reversal completes the vineyard response and echoes the previous chapter's closing saying.

keyVerses.text: It shall not be so among you; but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.
keyVerses.why: Jesus does not deny desire for significance; he replaces domination with service as its measure.

keyVerses.text: even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
keyVerses.why: Jesus's own approaching death grounds the community's alternative to Gentile-style domination.

questions.question: Is the vineyard owner endorsing unfair labor practices?
questions.answer: A denarius was a normal day's subsistence wage. The first workers receive exactly the agreed amount; the complaint is that late workers receive generosity too. The parable addresses kingdom reward and comparison, not a payroll policy for exploiting labor. It honors the owner's freedom to give enough rather than the first group's desire to make others receive less.

questions.question: Why are people still waiting late in the day?
questions.answer: The owner says they were standing because no one hired them, not because they refused work. Day laborers depended on being selected and could return home without food. The scene shifts moral attention from hours accumulated to vulnerability and a household's need for a full wage.

questions.question: What is the ‘evil eye’ in verse 15?
questions.answer: The Greek idiom asks whether their eye is evil because the owner is good. An ‘evil eye’ can signal envy, stinginess, or resentful perception. English ‘are you envious?’ carries the sense but loses Matthew's recurring eye language: how one sees another person's gift reveals the heart.

questions.question: Why does Matthew place a promotion request immediately after the death prediction?
questions.answer: The juxtaposition is the diagnosis. Jesus describes humiliation and death; the family hears an approaching kingdom as available cabinet seats. Matthew sometimes names the mother as speaker while Jesus answers the brothers, keeping their agency in view. Discipleship repeatedly misreads suffering glory as status opportunity.

questions.question: What is the ‘cup’ they claim they can drink?
questions.answer: The cup is a scriptural image for an allotted experience and often for suffering or judgment. Jesus will name his own cup in Gethsemane. James and John confidently accept a metaphor they do not yet understand; Jesus says they will share suffering without granting the requested rank.

questions.question: What does ‘ransom for many’ mean?
questions.answer: Lytron is a price of release, evoking liberation from slavery or captivity, while ‘for’ carries a representative or substitutionary force. ‘Many’ echoes Isaiah's servant and means a multitude rather than necessarily excluding ‘all.’ The verse interprets Jesus's death as liberating self-gift; later atonement models develop how that gift works.

questions.question: Why does Matthew have two blind men when Mark names one?
questions.answer: Matthew often doubles figures in miracle stories, while Mark focuses on Bartimaeus by name. Two witnesses may fit Matthew's narrative preference, but neither Gospel explains the difference. It is better to acknowledge distinct storytelling than invent an unseen second scene. Matthew's focus is their repeated Davidic cry and Jesus's compassion.

questions.question: What changes when the men call Jesus ‘Son of David’?
questions.answer: The title is royal and messianic. The crowd treats the shouting blind men as obstacles, but they identify the approaching king and force the procession to hear them. Jesus asks what they want, touches them from compassion, and their restored sight becomes following — literal vision and discipleship converge.

glossary.def: A common silver coin and conventional daily wage in the parable.
A scriptural image for an allotted fate, especially suffering and judgment in this context.
A payment or means of release from bondage, used to interpret the Son of Man's self-giving death.
